Prototype · two stages · built from the shipped bundle

What applies here

Two questions, in order, and never both on one screen: where on the river, then what applies there. Waters with one set of rules end to end — 96.37% of them, 11,523 of 11,957 — skip the first question entirely and open on the second. Only 27 waters in British Columbia have four or more stretches, and the Fraser has the most at twenty.

A rule is a type and its conditions, and the line you read is generated from them — never typed beside the numbers it describes. The fifteen types fall into six families, and those families are the headings below: somebody who wants to know whether they may keep a fish should not have to read eleven vessel rules to find out.

Getting this into the app

Everything above is drawn from the shipped bundle, so the question is not whether the data exists — it is which of these behaviours the app already has, and what has to be built. Four of the six steps are wiring; two are real decisions.

What already exists and needs nothing

  • runsOfSameRules in @app/core collapses adjacent sections that share a ruleset into stretches. That is the whole first stage, and the app already calls it for the water sheet.
  • rule.scope ships in the bundle as section | area, so the three-way split above — this water's rules, inherited, regional — needs no new query. So does rule.family, which groups each of those three into the sections you see, so the client carries no copy of the type-to-family mapping.
  • Every zone rule is already bound section-by-section, so a stretch's rules are the same one lookup the app makes today. Nothing about zone regulations is a special case — though getting there cost something. Binding every regional rule in the province took the rule-to-section relation from 2.7M pairs to 160.5 million, which interns down to +12.8 MB of bundle. That is what section_ruleset exists for.

What has to be built

01
The management unit has to reach the client.

The bundle deliberately does not carry it — administrative geography rides the tile, where every stream and lake feature has a mus attribute, and schema.sql is explicit that a rule-derived set belongs in the bundle and a containment fact does not. This prototype reads it from the atlas graph, which the app has no access to.

So the app must read mus off the tapped feature's properties. onPressFeature currently passes (layerId, featureId, lat, lon) and throws the properties away; it needs to pass them, or the map handle needs a propertiesOf(featureId). That is the only new data path in this whole list.

02
Order the rule list by origin, not by id.

Three groups, most specific first: written for this water, inherited down the tributary walk, then regional. The precedence line is not decoration — on the Fraser there are 84 regional rules against 26 of the river's own, and sorted together the general buries the specific.

03
Say that the specific overrides the general.

Half the regional rules end in "see water specific regulations table for exceptions". Showing a regional default beside a contradicting water-specific line, with nothing saying which governs, presents the reader with a contradiction and asks them to guess.

This is a claim about the law, not a layout choice. It should be stated once, in @app/core beside evaluate, so the sheet and anything else that ranks rules cannot disagree about it — the same argument that moved the gauge trust bands into a generated file.
04
Rules and Conditions have to share "where am I".

They do not today. Shell holds two separate selections — item for the water sheet and condSection for the conditions sheet — and switching tabs drops whichever the other tab was not using. A reader who taps a stretch of the Fraser to read its rules and then switches to Conditions arrives nowhere.

They are also different granularities, which is the part that needs deciding rather than coding:

tabselectsbecause
Rulesa stretch — a run of sections sharing a ruleset rules change at boundaries, not at every section
Conditionsa section one section, one gauge, one reading

The mapping is not symmetric: a stretch holds many sections, and only one of them is the one whose gauge you want. Going stretch → section needs a rule for which section represents it (the one carrying the gauge, if any; otherwise the downstream end). Going section → stretch is unambiguous — a section belongs to exactly one run.

Suggested shape: one place in Shell holding { item, section }, where section is always set and item is derived. Both tabs read it, both tabs write it, and the tab switch becomes a no-op rather than a reset. That also fixes the existing bug where opening a reach sheet from Conditions and returning to Map loses the reach.
05
The species filter needs the group table.

The four buckets this prototype filters by — trout & char, salmon, sturgeon, other — live in the export script, and the app's SpeciesGroup is a different thing entirely: it means the authority (provincial vs DFO), not the fish.

Which species a person considers one quarry is a judgement about people, not a fact about fish, so it belongs in curated data that both sides read — not written twice. The assertion that every code in the corpus lands in some bucket should move with it; it has already caught eleven codes that would otherwise have vanished from every filter but "all species".

06
Decide whether zone rules stay materialised.

Binding every regional rule to every section it covers is what makes all of the above a single lookup — but it tripled section_ruleset and cost about 22 MB, because every section in the province now carries its region's rules.

The alternative is to store them once per region and let the client union "rules for my region" with "rules for my section", which the tile's mus attribute already makes possible — and step 01 puts that attribute in the client's hands anyway. It is the cheaper artifact and the more complicated client. Worth settling before the schema is depended on, not after.

What this prototype still does not answer

  • Nine regional rules bind wider than the regulation says, because a within(area) extent can only add water — it cannot express "the Fraser watershed part of Region 5" or "all streams except the Peace". They are flagged in the entries and listed in that directory's README.
  • Eighteen rules carry an exception no extent subtracts. The carve-out is shown to the reader as text, which is honest but leaves prose doing a job the extents should do.
  • Nothing here renders unknown. A rule the resolver could not place must not draw as open, and this page has no state for it.
